sections.title: Welcome to the Origin of Money
sections.content:
Before banks, before coins, before even the concept of 'price' existed — humans needed a way to get what they didn't have.

Imagine you're a wheat farmer in ancient Mesopotamia. You've got tons of wheat, but you need shoes. Simple, right? Just find a shoemaker and trade.

Except... it's not that simple.

cards.front: What was the biggest problem with barter?
cards.back: Double coincidence of wants — both parties needed to want what the other had, at the exact same time.

cards.front: What is the 'Double Coincidence of Wants'?
cards.back: For a barter trade to work, Person A must want what Person B has, AND Person B must want what Person A has, at the same time and place.

cards.front: Why couldn't barter scale to large societies?
cards.back: With hundreds of goods, the number of possible exchange rates becomes unmanageable. 100 goods = 4,950 different exchange rates to remember!

cards.front: What are the 3 problems with barter?
cards.back:
1. Double coincidence of wants
2. No common measure of value (how many shoes = 1 cow?)
3. Indivisibility (can't cut a cow in half for change)

sections.title: Commodity Money: The First Solution
sections.content:
Humans needed something that EVERYONE agreed was valuable. Enter commodity money — physical goods that served as a medium of exchange.

Different civilizations chose different commodities:

• Salt — so valuable that Roman soldiers were paid in it
• Cowrie shells — used across Africa, South Asia, and East Asia
• Tobacco — used as currency in colonial America
• Cattle — the Latin word 'pecunia' (money) comes from 'pecus' (cattle)

These items worked because they were:
✓ Widely desired
✓ Relatively durable
✓ Portable (well, except cattle)
✓ Somewhat divisible

sections.text: The word SALARY comes from 'salarium' — Roman soldiers were literally paid in salt! Salt was so valuable it was called 'white gold.' That's where the phrase 'worth your salt' comes from.

panels.dialogue: I've watched them struggle for centuries. Trading sheep for grain, shells for tools. Always searching for what they need...
They needed something everyone agreed was valuable. Something they could carry, divide, and trust.
And so, from salt to shells to shiny metals — they began to discover ME. Money. The great connector.

sections.text: In Yap Island (Micronesia), money was made of giant stone discs called 'Rai stones' — some were 12 feet across and weighed 4 tons! Ownership was tracked by oral history since you obviously couldn't carry them around.

questions.question: What is the main problem with the barter system?
questions.explanation: Both parties needed to want exactly what the other had — at the same time. Imagine trying to trade your wheat for shoes, but the shoemaker doesn't want wheat!

questions.question: Where does the word 'salary' come from?
questions.explanation: Roman soldiers were paid in salt — 'salarium.' Salt was extremely valuable in the ancient world, used for preserving food and as a disinfectant.

questions.question: Which of these was NOT used as commodity money?
questions.explanation: Paper itself was never commodity money — it has no intrinsic value. Paper money came much later as a REPRESENTATION of value (promissory notes). Shells, salt, and tobacco were all used as commodity money.

questions.question: What makes something a good commodity money?
options: It must be rare and beautiful
It must be desired, durable, portable, and divisible
It must be approved by a government
It must be made of metal
questions.explanation: Good commodity money needs to be widely desired, durable (doesn't rot), portable (easy to carry), and divisible (can be split into smaller units).

questions.question: With 100 different goods in a barter economy, how many exchange rates would you need?
questions.explanation: The formula is n(n-1)/2. With 100 goods: 100 × 99 / 2 = 4,950 different exchange rates! Money solves this by giving everything ONE price.
